The practice of medicine has deteriorated a lot since I was a kid. Granted, we know more about some things, but I think changed incentives have swamped the benefits of greater scientific understanding. When we were kids, the family doctor had an independent practice. He (it was usually a man) would earn a good income, but he also had a lot of discretion in treating patients. He had time to educate and advise the patient about healthy living and to treat the patient as an entire human being who came to him in need of help or just reassurance. There were a few vaccines available against much-feared diseases like smallpox and polio, which were administered to screaming children to the relief of concerned parents. The doctor's notes were scribbled in notoriously poor handwriting and stuck in a manila folder to be filed in the front office until your next visit. Patients were billed at a reasonable rate for the doctor's time. Unless they were hospitalized and 'major medical' kicked in to cover 80%, there was no insurance company involved in the process. People budgeted for their occasional visits to the doctor and saved up for the costs associated with childbirth. Like owning a car, there were costs that you budgeted for, but insurance was there for the unexpected events that could bankrupt a family. If the doctor knew the family, he also might know which ones were in financial distress and make some adjustments to help them.

 

In contrast to the old-time doctor, today's typical family doctor is a cog in the wheel of a large medical system. The medical system is heavy with lawyers and its decisions guided and scrutinized by insurance companies. The patient is no longer Mr Jones or Mrs Wilson who live down the street and whose children go to school with the doctor's own children. They come in with ailments that carry codes that dictate treatment protocols and reimbursement rates. The doctor doesn't look the patient in the eye, because his or her eyes are glued to a screen and their hands are typing away into the computer system. The computer undoubtedly prompts the doctor regarding 'correct' protocols of vaccines, pills, therapy, surgery, etc. The protocol is cost effective and sufficiently effective medically to keep the patient alive and paying premiums and co-pays. It isn't tailored to the patient and can't tell when the patient is just scared or lonely. The doctor can't risk diverging from the protocol, even if they suspect it isn't the best for the patient. To do so invites scrutiny, disciplinary action, or withdrawal of support should the decision lead to a malpractice claim. The doctor is no longer free to provide care to the best of their ability. They provide a service that is defined as appropriate by the expert panels, lawyers, and accountants. Patients come in with insurance cards and the expectation that costs are largely covered. They have no knowledge of the costs of procedures and no influence over them apart from declining treatment. They are billed at ridiculous rates as medical systems attempt to recover costs associated with uninsured patients and expensive technology. Insurance companies negotiate them down and the patient is stuck with whatever is left. Since the initial bill was huge, and the patient typically has responsibility for a percentage of it, the resulting bill can also be huge. And those HIPPA-protected medical records? Now that they are digitally entered into a system, they can be anywhere - processed in India, hacked in Russia, leaked in China.

 

Who pays for all this oversight and 'efficiency'? We do - with our excessive premiums, co-pays, and taxes to provide care for the uninsured. LIke anything else, medicine involves a balance of effectiveness and efficiency. I think patients are suffering a lack of effectiveness because the current system is driven primarily by efficiency and profit for the providers of technology and medicines. Doctors don't answer to patients. They answer to those who dictate efficiency. It is very telling that so many doctors advise their own children against careers in medicine.
